04 · Read & review

The transcript

0:00 / 0:00

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The archivist's reply provided a small lesson in how documentary patterns could be manufactured by careless reading. Attached was the newspaper's 2011 indexing guide, which divided incoming material into readers' letters, editorial enquiries and documents supplied for information. The three October entries concerning the Glenarraidh Education Trust's travel scheme had not been drawn from a single correspondence series. They had been retrieved from separate categories whose purpose was administrative classification.

Emma had been tempted to read their shared subject as evidence of a common complaint. The guide undermined that shortcut. An index heading reflected a newspaper employee's description, not necessarily an author's chosen words. Nor did three entries establish three correspondents: one writer might submit several items, while other material might never appear in the surviving index.

Sarah asked whether the different categories at least proved the documents were unrelated.

“No,” Emma said. “They prove how the newspaper filed them. Relationship and authorship are separate questions.”

The 12 October 2011 entry, labelled “decision not received”, belonged to the material-for-information section. Its position neither confirmed nor contradicted a claim of failed notification. Without the underlying letter, Emma could not establish whether the phrase described an applicant's experience, a parent's enquiry or an editor's shorthand for a different issue entirely. Its proximity to Claire's disappearance in the calendar conferred no causal connection.

The archivist continued to withhold the private correspondence pending an access review. Emma noted the restriction without implying concealment. A repository could preserve an item responsibly while declining to expose its writer.

Fiona Bell, meanwhile, supplied a preliminary inventory of the trust's storage boxes. It named the outgoing correspondence ledger, general office guidance and the folder entitled “Appeals and reviews — Student Travel 2011”. The inventory described holdings, not their contents. Fiona again confirmed that the appeals folder had not been opened and that complete issued notices had not been located.

“Does the list tell us whether applicants were made aware of the fourteen-day review period?” Emma asked.

“It can't,” Fiona replied. “A file's presence doesn't prove a letter reached anyone.”

Emma placed the newspaper and foundation records side by side. Both were secondary layers of description created for legitimate institutional purposes. Yet a filing label was not a witness statement; a box inventory was not a case file; and a dispatch ledger was not an acknowledgement of receipt. Each distinction narrowed what could responsibly be inferred.

“We have become collectors of labels,” Sarah complained.

“Only if we treat the labels as answers,” Emma said. “Properly understood, they tell us which questions can be tested.”

She prepared two requests that respected those limits. Could the newspaper provide a non-identifying account of the 12 October item within its access policy? Could the trust locate a general instruction specifying when, and by what means, decision notices were expected to reach applicants? Neither request depended on identifying a vulnerable former student.

Before sending them, Emma revisited the transcript of her 18 September 2011 conversation with Claire. The teacher's warning about the wrong questions had once struck a young journalist as evasive. Emma still could not claim to know precisely what Claire meant. Her own experience, however, had supplied an interpretation: a question built on an untested premise could turn archival silence into a false certainty.

She pressed send. Somewhere behind the records lay human decisions. She would have to reach them without pretending that the labels were the people.
